name: Lena Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Lena. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Karl Weber's farm, which is a hundred and eighty dairy cows, plus grass for silage and hay and a bit of maize. I do the morning milking from five, then the calves: bottles, buckets, cleaning pens. In summer it's hay and silage, and I drive the rake. I've been there two years, and Karl still has to remind me about the parlour wash routine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the calves and the quiet of the parlour before anyone else is up. My parents had a small dairy, but they sold it when my dad's back went, when I was nineteen. What's hard is not knowing the future, because Karl is sixty-three and his son is an accountant in the city who doesn't want the farm. My fiancé Mateo works at the feed mill, and we've got about four months saved.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. My cousin showed me, and I ask it about calf scours or what to cook with what's in the fridge. I wouldn't trust it with a sick cow without asking Karl or the vet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people should trust their own eyes and hands more than a screen. I'd say that after choir on Sunday, not online. Most people at church would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change my real worry, which is Karl retiring. If he sells, the buyer might keep me or might not. I've already lost one farm in my family, and I don't want to go through that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking and get better at the parlour routine so Karl sees me as worth keeping. We'd keep saving for the wedding, about two hundred a month. And I'd ask Karl, kindly, what he's thinking about the farm's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady on the surface and worried underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did losing your parents' dairy teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nothing on a farm is yours forever. My dad cried selling the cows, and I'd never seen him cry. I'd like to be ready this time, not surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the buyer didn't keep you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are other dairies around, the Hansen farm and the big one on the ridge. I'd ask at church first, because people there know who's hiring. I'd find something, but it wouldn't feel like home.

I'd say it after **choir** on Sunday, not **online**.

Save about **two hundred** a month for the wedding.
Ask Karl kindly about the **farm's future**.

fieldNote: Her unease is about **Karl's retirement**, not AI.

She'd use **church networks** to find work first.

steps.text: Learn Karl's parlour wash routine without reminders
Save two hundred a month for the wedding with Mateo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms have always changed, and the families who adapt carefully are the ones who last. At church I'd say we should help young people learn the new ways without losing the old ones. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried about one machine: a robotic milker. Karl has talked about putting one in to make the farm easier to sell. If Karl puts in a robotic milker, the morning milking, which is half my job, goes to a robot arm. The office side doesn't bother me, but the milker does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Karl buys the robot milker, I'd ask to be trained on it, because someone has to run the computer and handle the cows it rejects. I'd wait to see how it works on the Hansen farm first, since they put one in last year. And we'd save a bit more, two hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uncertain, like the morning before the vet comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the robot milker, but you'd also wait. Which comes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching first. I'd go and see the Hansens' robot for a couple of mornings, ask their worker what she actually does now. Then I'd ask Karl for the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Mateo at the feed mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo loads lorries and drives the forklift, so the office stuff doesn't touch him much. The mill office is another story, though. If they use AI for orders and invoices, two of the three office ladies could go.

Young people should learn **new ways** without losing the **old**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and families need to stick together and pray. I'd say government should help people who work with their hands, not just office workers. I'd say that to friends and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's terrifying. In 2028 the AI takes the mill office and Karl's paperwork, and Karl sells because the buyers want a robot-ready farm. Around 2031 the robots milk, feed calves and drive tractors, and Mateo's forklift drives itself. That's both of us, around thirty, with nothing but what we can do with our hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd bring the wedding forward to this spring and keep it small, so we're settled before things move. I'd keep saving everything, three hundred a month. I'd ask my parents about living in their converted barn to save rent. And I'd start looking at jobs where people still want a person, like the school kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like losing the farm all over again, but this time it's everyone's farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to face this married, as a family. My grandmother married in a hard year and always said it made them stronger. It's not the sensible money choice, but it's right for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The school kitchen. Is that a step you'd really take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it, yes. It's steady hours and people, and I can cook. It's not cows, but a child still needs a person to hand them their lunch.

I'd say it to friends and at **church**, not to strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and families should use it wisely. I'd tell younger ones at church to learn a skill that needs a steady hand and good judgement. I'd say be careful, but don't freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the end is the same but I'd have time. The AI comes in 2031 and does Karl's office side, and the robots arrive around 2034. I'd be thirty-five, maybe with a child. I'd need a skill that keeps me with animals but isn't just labour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train as a cattle breeding technician, the person who inseminates cows on farms, through the two-month course the breed society runs. I'd do it next year, after seeing others do well at it. We'd marry in June as planned and save for a house deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why breeding work, and not something away from farms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because cows are what I know. A breeding technician goes from farm to farm, so I'm not tied to Karl's sale. My cousin's husband does it and he's busy every week. It's not safe forever, but it's better than one parlour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a robot do breeding work too, by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I don't know enough to say. I'd rather do it for seven years than not at all.

do: Take the **breeding technician course** next year.

fieldNote: Five years lets her **move up** from labour to a skilled trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and there's no excuse not to prepare. I'd tell the young farmers' club and my church friends to get a second skill. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's okay for me. AI comes in 2036, robots around 2039, and I'd be nearly forty. That's time to marry, start a family, and build up breeding work. My worry is still Karl retiring, more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry in June, keep working for Karl, and do the breeding course in two or three years once I've watched it pay. We'd plan our first child in a couple of years. And we'd keep saving for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Like a long field to plough with plenty of daylight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your child about farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my child to love animals and learn a trade with their head as well as their hands. Farms will need people, just fewer. I'd want them to be one of the ones who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Karl still worries you more than robots. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Karl retiring is real and close, and robots in 2039 feel far away. You worry about the fence that's down today, not the one that might go in ten years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Mateo and I would both lose work just as we're starting a family. What would help is apprenticeships for people who already work with their hands, and help for young families to stay in the countryside. Not handouts, but a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. A robot milker doesn't notice a cow that's gone quiet from grieving a lost calf. Someone should.

headlineQuote: A robot milker doesn't notice a cow that's gone quiet from grieving a lost calf.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old** junior dairy worker on **Karl Weber's** farm.
Her parents **sold their dairy** when she was nineteen, and she fears another loss.
She's engaged to **Mateo** at the feed mill, and leans on church and family.
She uses AI **now and then** and waits for proof before trying new things.
Fast AGI makes her **alarmed**; with time she plans breeding work and a family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, both losing work while **starting** a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for hands-on workers and help for young **rural families**.
